queries: [Page 105] 0003. A separate industrial line accepts food processing wastewater seasonally from Eckert Cold Storage from about May through November. Eckert Cold Storage processes frozen vegetables (e.g., cabbage and a variety of peppers), and discharges primarily wastewater from the cutting and washing of these vegetables. At times, the food processing wastewater is mixed with wastewaters from clean-up of the processing equipment, freezer defrost waters, and cooling towers. The food processing wastewater is stored and aerated in a lined pond, and then applied to agricultural fields when needed. Use of land disposal onto agricultural fields is being phased out as the City is using more of its land for commercial development. A. Description of Wastewater and Biosolids Treatment and Controls The Facility has a design average dry weather flow capacity of 9.87 MGD and its treatment process is divided into two parallel treatment systems, the north and south treatment systems. Primary treatment is identical in both systems and consists of mechanical screening, aerated grit removal, and primary sedimentation. At the north plant, the primary effluent may undergo additional treatment through two biotowers with high-rate plastic media (currently out of service). The secondary treatment processes for both treatment systems are the same, consisting of conventional activated sludge, including nitrification-denitrification, followed by secondary sedimentation. chunks.text: Primary sedimentation is to remove the suspended solids (SS) by controlling the water flow velocity. It is required the settling time of SS shorter than the water travelling time in the tank. The SS with low density (1.1 g/mL and 1.5 g/mL) or small size but high density (1.5 g/mL) is the target pollutants to be removed in primary clarification. Most abundant MPs in the wastewater is PET followed by PE and PP (Fig. 2b ). The density of PET is between 0.96 and 1.45 g/mL. It is predicted that the primary sedimentation would catch the MPs consist of PET. However, PE and PP are difficult to be removed as they have density lower than water. Hence, wastewater containing large amount of moderate-density MPs would have high MPs removal during primary treatment.

chunks.text: The secondary clarifier is a 10-layer non-reactive system labelled from the bottom to the top. It has a total height of 4 m, and occupies a surface area of 1500 m 2 and a volume of 6000 m 3 . The tank is fed from the 6th, treated water is harvested from the 10th, and the settled sludge flows out from the first layer. A fraction of the sludge flows out of the system in the form of waste at a flow rate of 385 m 3 /d, corresponding to a biomass age of 9 days, while the other fraction is recycled externally to the first tank at a rate of 18,446 m 3 /d. The biological processes occurring in both biological reactors are simulated using the IWA Activated Sludge Model No. 1 (ASM1) proposed by [47] . This model uses thirteen state variables to track the fate of biodegradable, non-biodegradable, soluble, insoluble, nitrogen, and carbon materials. These state variables are linked to eight degradation bioprocesses occurring in biological reactors.

chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.text: Screens and grit removal are widely employed in WWTPs as they enhance the operation and maintenance of subsequent treatment units. Recent innovations in pretreatment technologies have brought the heavy cost of grit in WWTPs operations lower which has been considered an unavoidable burden. For example, based on advanced Grit Management™, Headcell® grit separation system was developed to achieve optimum grit removal for more than 30 years in the UK and USA. Headcell® is capable of achieving 95% removal of all grit 75 μm and larger. Because of its no-moving part design involving a hydraulically driven system, it delivers grit removal over a wide range of flows in a much smaller energy footprint than the conventional removal systems (Barter and Sherony, 2011) . Table 5 lists several such advanced technologies currently being considered for pilot, demonstration, and full-scale operations in the North America.

chunks.citation: Badawi, AK et al. (2022). Advanced wastewater treatment process using algal photo-bioreactor associated with dissolved-air flotation system: A pilot-scale demonstration. J WATER PROCESS ENG.
chunks.text: Within the framework of this study, an algal photo-bioreactor combined with a dissolved air flotation system (DAF) was used for the removal of COD, BOD 5 , TSS, TN and TP from primary treated wastewater. The optimum operating conditions for the algal photo-bioreactor were determined through batch experiments, which are pH 7, temperature 25 • C, light intensity 90 μmol m − 2 S − 1 and mixing rate 100 rpm. Those optimal conditions were used in a scaled-up pilot plant treatment system to treat primary treated wastewater from ZENIN WWTP-Egypt. The operation has shown significant results where COD, BOD 5 , TSS, TN and TP have been removal with efficiencies of 56.4%, 61%, 59.2%, 48.3% and 51.7% respectively. These findings have been compared with previous studies. These findings proved the efficacy of algal-bacterial integrated treatment systems combined with DAF as a wastewater treatment technology that does not require any additional tertiary treatment to release the effluent to sewer systems.

chunks.text: Nitrification is an essential process for nitrogen removal from wastewater, comprising two steps, i.e., the oxidation of ammonium (NH 4 + ) to nitrite (NO 2 − ), and then to nitrate (NO 3 − ). In a wastewater treatment system, nitrification usually occurs at a neutral pH (∼7) with NO 3 − as the final product when the oxygen supply is unlimited. Nitrification at an acidic pH was recently suggested as a novel process for wastewater treatment. At a slightly acidic pH range (4.5−5.5), it was found that the end product of nitrification tends to be NO 2 − instead of NO 3 − , even with high dissolved oxygen (DO > 4 mg O 2 / L). 1,2 However, acidic nitrification without considerable NO 2 − accumulation has also been widely reported in literature. 3−5 Tarre et al. 4 observed NO 3 − accumulation in suspended-and attached-biomass reactors at pH of ∼4, in which nitriteoxidizing bacteria (NOB) Nitrobacter existed in large aggregates.

chunks.text: However, these processes are costly, require high energy consumption and generally produce secondary waste which cannot remove the pollutants completely and then puts more pressure on the environment (Ghafari et al., 2008; Kapoor and Viraraghavan, 1997) . In contrast, biological treatment is generally regarded as a better choice for nitrate removal from wastewater due to its advantages of complete contaminants removal, economical and energy-saving. Currently, the complete denitrification process is widely applied for nitrate-containing wastewater treatment (Gu et al., 2015; Song et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020) . However, the traditional complete denitrification process (Eqs. ( 1 ) and ( 2 )) still presents some shortcomings, including high operational costs due to external organic carbon source requirements (Gu et al., 2015; Song et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020) , large amounts of sludge yields and inevitable greenhouse gas emission, etc. (Du et al., 2016b) . Partial denitrification (PD) refers to the process of controlling NO 3 − -N reduced to NO 2 − -N without further reducing to nitrogen gas (N 2 ).

chunks.text: Wastewater from food processing units usually comes from non-processing functions and has the characteristics of complex composition, a wide variety of pollutants, and large fluctuations with seasons and types of raw materials. Most of the food wastewater contains high concentrations of organic pollutants, such as chemical oxygen demand (COD), biological oxygen demand (BOD), total suspended solids (TSS), nitrogen, phosphorus, and other different chemicals, as well as nutrients such as carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids (Natasha et al., 2020) . The treatment of food wastewater is necessary because direct discharge will seriously pollute the surrounding land and surface water, and lead to the eutrophication of water (Wang et al., 2021a) . Sustainable development is now driving a rapid shift in focus in the wastewater and organic waste sector, from a "removal and treatment" approach to the recovery and reuse of "water, energy and materials" (Capson-Tojo et al., 2020) . Food wastewater has a great potential for resource recovery and reuse because of its rich nutrients, low heavy metals, and toxic pollutants (Costa et al., 2022) .

Specifically, plants A, B, and C experienced a reduction in CFP of 7.55%, 9.5%, and 10.59%, respectively. This is because greater particulate settling in the primary clarifier results in lower CO 2 emissions from microbial respiration and higher waste sludge  contents in the AD process (Gori et al., 2011 (Gori et al., , 2013)) . In terms of CO 2 emissions, the AD ranked third after PG, with 0.019, 0.039, and 0.34 kg CO 2 /kg COD rem. for plants A, B, and C, respectively. Plant C received almost 5.6 times lower COD than plant A, resulting in higher COD removal (78.75%) and concurrently larger CO 2 emissions.

chunks.text: In the activated sludge process the majority of biological solids removed in the secondary sedimentation tank are recycled (returned sludge). The feedback of most of the cell yields from the sedimentation tank encourages rapid adsorption of the pollutants in the incoming settled sewage and also serves to stabilize the operation over a wide range of dilution rates and substrate concentrations imposed by fluctuations in the flow and strength of the wastewater. Secondary treatment processes can remove up to 95 per cent of the BOD and suspended solids entering the process, as well as significant amounts of heavy metals and certain organic compounds which could otherwise cause the deterioration of chemical and ecological quality of receiving waters [10, 53] . Conventional wastewater treatment usually ends with secondary treatment which cannot efficiently remove all the different compounds found in sewage and therefore treated effluents are one of the main sources of persistent micropollutants in the environment [1, 62] . For water reuse, tertiary treatment is needed to provide additional removal of contaminants such as microbial pathogens, particulates, or nutrients, and advanced treatment processes are employed when wastewater is to be reclaimed for reuse, depending on the type of use and quality requirements [49] .

chunks.text: A mass of 300 kg of screenings was sampled from the municipal wastewater treatment plant of Bourg-en-Bresse (Region Rhône-   Alpes, France). The sample was taken to the laboratory where it was homogenized and divided into 20 sub-samples of 8 kg.
